procedural_history.originating_court: Magistrate Court (inferred from the text mentioning appeal from a Magistrate to a Sessions Judge)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Notification conferring power on the Special Judge to try the case (challenged by the petitioners).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court transferred the case to a Special Judge and conferred power on the Special Judge to try the case, without hearing the petitioners. The High Court's judgment was upheld.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioners approached the Supreme Court because they were prejudiced by the High Court's action, as it took away their right of appeal from a Magistrate to a Sessions Judge. The Supreme Court dismissed the special leave petitions, upholding the High Court's decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether a law that brings about a change in the 'forum' for trial affects pending actions, and whether a litigant has a vested right in the matter of the 'forum'.

law.fact: A law that changes the 'forum' (the court or tribunal for a trial) is generally considered a change in procedural law, not substantive law.
law.source: 5. On the plain language of Sections 110-A and II 0-F there should be no difficulty in taking the view that the change in law was merely a change of forum i.e. a change of adjectival or procedural law and not of substantive law.

law.fact: A litigant has a vested right to a cause of action, but generally does not have a vested right to a particular forum before proceedings are initiated.
law.source: He will have a vested right of action but not a vested right of forum.

law.fact: The general principle for pending actions is that a law changing the forum does not affect them unless the new law shows a clear intention to the contrary.
law.source: 18. It may be stated at the outset that the general principle is that a law which brings about a change in the forum does not affect pending actions unless intention to the contrary is clearly shown.

law.fact: Such a contrary intention can be shown by an express provision in the new law that mandates the transfer of pending cases to the new forum.
law.source: One of lhe modes by which such an intention is shown is by making a provision for change-over of proceedings, from the court or the tribunal where they are pending to the court or the tribunal which under the new law gets jurisdiction to try them.

law.fact: Once a remedy has been availed of (i.e., proceedings have commenced), the right to that forum can be treated as having crystallized into a vested substantive right.
law.source: where the remedy had already been availed of (under an existing statutory provision), the right may be treated as having crystalised into a vested substantive right.

application.fact: The Supreme Court distinguished between situations where legal proceedings had not yet been started and those where they were already pending when the law on the forum changed.
application.source: From a perusal of the conclusions drawn in lhe above judgments, we are inclined to accept the contention, that change of 'forum' could be substantive or procedural. It may well be procedural when the remedy was yet to be availed of, but where the remedy had already been availed of(under an existing statutory provision), the right may be treated as having crystalised into a vested substantive right.

application.fact: For cases not yet filed, the Court affirmed that a change of forum is procedural and operates retrospectively. The litigant has no vested right to the old forum and must file their case in the new one.
application.source: It is a well-established proposition that such a change of law operates retrospectively and the person has to go to the new forum even if his cause of action or right of action accrued prior to the change of forum.

application.fact: For cases already pending, the Court held that the right to the original forum becomes a vested right. Therefore, the change in law does not affect these pending actions.
application.source: a law which brings about a change in the 'forum', does not affect pending actions, unless intention to the contrary is clearly shown.

application.fact: The Court clarified that this vested right in the forum for a pending case can only be taken away if the new amending law, by express words or necessary implication, mandates the transfer of such proceedings to the newly established forum.
application.source: unless the amending provision by express words, or by necessary implication, mandates the transfer of proceedings to the 'forum' introduced by the amendment. the 'forum' postulated by the unamended provision, would continue to have the jurisdiction to adjudicate upon pending matters (matters tiled before amendment).

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that while a litigant has no vested right in a particular forum before a case is filed, the right to that forum becomes a vested right once proceedings have been initiated. Consequently, a law that changes the forum does not affect pending actions, and the original court retains jurisdiction, unless the new law explicitly or by necessary implication provides for the transfer of those pending cases.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a law that brings about a change in the 'forum' for trial affects pending actions, and whether a litigant has a vested right in the matter of the 'forum'.
appellant_arguments: A litigant has a vested right in the forum of trial.
A pending legal proceeding or remedy, before an amendment altered the forum, should continue to be adjudicated in the original forum.
This continuation in the original forum is supported by Sections 6(c) and (e) of the relevant act, unless the amending law expressly or by necessary implication states otherwise.
The transfer of jurisdiction from one court to another due to a legislative amendment should not apply to their pending case.
respondent_arguments: A litigant has no vested right in a matter of procedure, and the choice of 'forum' is a procedural matter.
An alteration in procedure, such as a change of forum, has an implied retrospective effect and applies to pending actions.
Therefore, the opposing party cannot claim that the change of 'forum' has adversely affected any of their vested rights.

cases.principle: Cited in the context of the applicability of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, which covers a wide field and saves a wide range of proceedings upon the repeal of an enactment.

Pending cases, although instituted under an old Act, are governed by the new procedure under an amended law. However, any procedure that was correctly adopted and concluded under the old law cannot be reopened to apply the new procedure.

cases.case_name: Delhi Cloth and General Mills Co. Ltd. v. CIT
cases.principle: Provisions which affect a right that is in existence at the time of the passing of a statute are not to be applied retrospectively, unless there is an express enactment or necessary intendment to do so.
As a general rule, an amended law relating to procedure operates retrospectively.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: All procedural laws are retrospective unless the legislature expressly states to the contrary; therefore, the procedural law in force must be applied at the date when a suit or proceeding comes on for trial or disposal, as no party has a vested right to a particular proceeding or forum.
obiter: Prohibitive or negative words in a statute are ordinarily indicative of a mandatory nature.
Section 6 of the General Clauses Act ensures that pending proceedings under an unamended provision remain unaffected by its repeal.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court affirmed the High Court's decision, holding that there is no substance in the petitioners' objections. The court's reasoning relies on established legal precedent, which dictates that the choice of 'forum' for a trial is a matter of procedure, not a vested substantive right. Consequently, a legislative amendment that changes the forum for trial is considered procedural and applies retrospectively to pending actions.
legal_tests_applied: The distinction between a substantive vested right and a matter of procedure, with the 'forum' of a trial being classified as procedural.

The principle that an alteration in procedural law, such as a change of forum, has an implied retrospective effect and applies to pending legal actions unless the amending statute expressly or by necessary implication states otherwise.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's central claim that a litigant possesses a vested right in the 'forum' for their trial.
The court did not accept the argument that a pending proceeding must continue in its original forum after a legislative amendment, because the change was deemed procedural in nature.
The court found no reason to take a view different from the one taken by the High Court, effectively endorsing the lower court's application of the law on this issue.
why_respondent_won: The court's decision aligns with the respondent's argument that a litigant has no vested right in a matter of procedure.
The court accepted the legal position that the choice of 'forum' is a procedural matter.

The court implicitly endorsed the principle that a change in forum, being a procedural alteration, has a retrospective effect and applies to pending cases, thereby negating any claim of adverse effect on the appellant's vested rights.
